transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because I just feel like I can’t settle inside myself anymore. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like I’m sitting there and my body is telling me I need to get up, do something, move on to the next thing, even when I’m exhausted and I know I should just sit still. I feel worn out, but at the same time I can’t really rest. It’s like being uncomfortable in my own skin, and it’s gotten to the point where I thought, “I can’t keep doing this without talking to someone.”
Have you started or changed the dose of any medications recently, especially antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or other psychiatric medications?

I don’t think so… not that I can think of. I mean, I’m trying to remember everything because sometimes I get mixed up with what’s what, but I haven’t started anything like that recently, and I don’t believe any doses were changed. No antipsychotic medicines or nausea medicines that I know of. If you mean something over-the-counter or vitamins or something, I’d have to think more carefully, but nothing like what you mentioned comes to mind.

When you feel this need to move or can't settle, is it mainly a physical, bodily urge to be in motion, or do you also notice a lot of worried or fearful thoughts running through your mind at the same time?

It feels mostly physical, I think. I mean, I do get frustrated by it, because I’ll be sitting there thinking, “Why can’t I just stay put like a normal person?” but the main thing is this feeling in my body, like I can’t settle inside my own skin. Like I have to jump up and do the next thing, move to the next room, start something else, even when I’m completely worn out and I know I should be sitting still.

It’s not so much that I’m sitting there scared of something specific, or thinking something terrible is going to happen. It’s more like my body is pushing me, like there’s this uncomfortable buzzing or pressure that says, “Get up, get moving.” And then if I try to ignore it, I feel even more uncomfortable, like I’m trapped in the chair or in myself, if that makes sense.
When you do get up and move around, does that actually make the uncomfortable feeling go away or lessen, even temporarily?

It might ease it for a moment, yes, but it doesn’t really go away in any lasting way. Like, if I get up, I’m not stuck in the chair anymore, so that trapped feeling is a little less intense, but then I’m just moving on to the next thing. I’ll stand up, go into another room, start doing something, then almost right away I feel like I need to do something else again.

That’s the part that’s been so exhausting. It’s not like I get up, walk around, and then I feel calm and can sit back down comfortably. It’s more like I’m chasing the feeling, if that makes sense. My body keeps telling me, “Get up, do the next thing,” even when I’m worn out and I know I should just sit still. I came in because I feel like I can’t settle inside my own skin anymore.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you also been feeling persistently sad, down, or empty, or have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

I’m not really sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I’ve been upset and worn out by everything, and I get discouraged because it’s frustrating to feel like I can’t just relax, but I don’t think it’s the same as being sad all day or feeling empty.

As far as interest in things… I haven’t really noticed a big loss of interest, at least not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. It’s more that I have trouble settling into anything long enough to enjoy it properly, if that makes sense. But I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped caring about things I used to like or that nothing gives me pleasure anymore. Not that I’ve clearly noticed.
Are you currently taking any medications at all, even ones you've been on for a while, such as anti-nausea drugs, antipsychotics, or other prescriptions?

Um… I’m not sure how to answer that completely off the top of my head. I don’t think I’m taking anything like what you mentioned, like nausea medicine or antipsychotic medicine, at least not that I know of. I don’t want to say the wrong thing, though, because I know sometimes medications have names I don’t really recognize.

I’m not currently thinking of any prescription that would fit that, but I’d probably need to check my bottles or a list to be absolutely sure. I don’t want to accidentally leave something out just because I don’t remember the name right now.
Do you notice that this restless, can't-settle feeling is worse in the evening or at night, particularly when you're lying down to rest, compared to earlier in the day?

I don’t know that I’d say it’s only worse at night, exactly. It’s more like the feeling is just there — that sense that I can’t settle inside my own skin. Even if I’m tired and I know I should just sit still or rest, something in me keeps pushing like, “Get up, do the next thing,” and then I do, and then it starts all over again.

When I’m lying down, I notice it because I’m supposed to be resting, so it feels more obvious, I guess. But I came in because it’s not just a bedtime thing. It’s this constant uncomfortable urge to move on to the next thing, even when I’m worn out. It feels like I can’t get comfortable being still.
When you feel this need to move, is the uncomfortable sensation mainly in your legs, or do you feel it more throughout your whole body?

It’s not mainly my legs, no. I mean, I do move my legs sometimes, but the feeling itself isn’t like it’s located there, if that makes sense. It’s more my whole body, or almost like it’s under my skin everywhere.

That’s really why I came in — because I feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. I’ll be worn out, and I know I should just sit still, but there’s this push in me like I have to get up and do the next thing, and then the next thing after that. It’s not just my legs needing to move. It’s more like all of me can’t come to rest.
Have you ever, at any point in your life, taken an antipsychotic medication or a strong anti-nausea drug like metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, even briefly or a long time ago?

I honestly don’t know for sure. Those names don’t sound familiar to me — metoclopramide or prochlor… prochlorperazine, I don’t think I’ve heard those before, at least not in a way I remember.

I don’t believe I’ve ever been on an antipsychotic medicine, but I’m a little hesitant to give you a flat no because over the years, you know, doctors hand you prescriptions and sometimes I don’t keep the names straight. Especially if it was something brief a long time ago, I might not remember the exact name. I don’t want to accidentally say no if there was some one-time medication I took and didn’t realize what category it was in.

But as far as I know sitting here right now, nothing like that comes to mind.
When did this feeling of not being able to settle in your body first start—was it something new that began recently, or has it been building up over months or years?

It’s not brand-new, no. The point where it really started causing real trouble was after my husband died — that was about a year and ten months ago now.

I mean, I don’t know if there were little bits of it before that that I just didn’t pay attention to, but since then it’s been much harder to ignore. It’s been building and hanging around since that time, not like one day last week it suddenly appeared. That’s the time I connect it to, because that’s when I started feeling like I really couldn’t settle in myself anymore.
Since your husband passed away, do you find yourself frequently longing for him or having a hard time accepting that he's gone, even now?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… he was my husband, so of course I miss him, and there are moments where it still feels strange that he’s not here. But I don’t know if I’d call it “not accepting” it, if that makes sense.

I know he’s gone. I’m not walking around thinking he’s going to come back, or anything like that. But emotionally, some days it still catches me. So I guess I do long for him in the normal sense of missing someone you loved, but I’m not sure whether it’s the kind of longing you’re asking about.

Does this restless, can't-settle feeling tend to get noticeably worse specifically when you're thinking about your husband or reminded of him, or does it feel pretty much the same intensity regardless of whether you're thinking about him or not?

It doesn’t feel like it only happens when I’m thinking about him. I mean, reminders of him can upset me, of course, but this restless feeling is more like it’s just there in me.

That’s really why I came in — I feel like I can’t settle inside my own skin anymore. Like I should be able to sit down and rest, especially when I’m worn out, but instead there’s this push in me like I have to get up and do the next thing, or move on to something else, even if I don’t actually have anything important to do.

So no, I wouldn’t say it’s specifically tied to thoughts of my husband. It can be there whether I’m thinking about him or not. It’s more this constant “I can’t sit still inside myself” feeling.

I’m sorry, I’m not sure what you’re asking me there — or maybe I missed the question. If you mean whether I’ve noticed a clear pattern to it, I don’t know that I have, beyond what I was saying before. It’s sort of hard for me to pin down neatly, because once I start trying to describe it, I feel like I go in circles a little.

I can tell you what it feels like, but if you’re asking about something more specific, you might have to put it another way for me.
Has this constant urge to move made it hard for you to do things like get through work tasks, run errands, or spend time with friends and family?

Yes… yes, it has. More than I like to admit, honestly. I’m not working anymore, so it’s not “work tasks” in the job sense, but there are still things I’m supposed to keep up with, and I just… don’t, or I start them and leave them half-done because I’m up and down and onto the next thing.

My family has had to step in with bills and paperwork, which is embarrassing at my age. I’ll have things sitting there that need attention, and somehow I can’t just sit long enough and go through them properly. Then somebody has to come help me sort it out, or remind me, or basically take over.

And it’s affected other people too. At church, or with the garden, I’ll say I can help with something or I’m supposed to be responsible for a piece of it, and then I either drop the ball or change what I’m doing or don’t follow through the way I meant to. People have had to redo plans or cover for things I didn’t get done. They’re kind about it, but I can tell. I can tell they don’t feel like they can count on me the same way, and that hurts because those groups matter to me.

I feel really embarrassed by it. It’s not that I don’t care. I do care. Sometimes that makes it worse, because I’m watching myself be unreliable with things and people I actually care about.

I don’t mean every single minute has been exactly the same, but the trouble from it — not being able to sit and handle things, making a mess of responsibilities, needing other people to step in — that’s been going on pretty much since after he died. It didn’t just pass after a few months. It’s still here, and it’s been causing real trouble for nearly two years now.

I’ve had stressful periods in life like anybody has, but I can’t honestly point to another time and say, “Yes, it was just like this.” I don’t want to tell you something just because it sounds like it would fit. This has stood out to me because it’s been so hard to get a handle on, and because other people have had to help me so much.

So I guess the most honest answer is… I haven’t noticed that same pattern before, or at least I can’t remember it clearly enough to say. If there’s a more specific example you mean, you might have to ask me that way.

I guess the simplest way to say it is… I came in because I feel like I can’t settle inside my own skin anymore. That’s what it feels like. It’s not just being “busy,” if that makes sense. It feels more like I’m driven from the inside. I’ll sit down and almost right away I feel like I can’t stay there, like I have to jump up again. And sometimes I’m worn out while I’m doing it, so it doesn’t even feel useful. It’s just this constant unsettled feeling, like my body won’t let me rest.

I’m sorry, I’m not sure exactly what you mean by “since your…” — since my husband died, do you mean?

If you’re asking whether there’s still something specific going on because of that, I don’t know how to answer cleanly. I mean, his being gone is still his being gone, if that makes sense, but I’m not sure what part of that you’re asking about — whether there are still practical things from it, or whether I’m still reacting to the loss, or whether something new is keeping it going.

I don’t want to guess and give you the wrong answer. If you ask it a little more specifically, I think I can try to tell you better.

Right now, are there still specific practical changes from your husband's death—like new financial responsibilities, living arrangements, or day-to-day roles—that you're actively dealing with, or has most of that settled down at this point?

I don’t really know how to separate that out, honestly. I mean, there are still… things that are different because he’s not here, of course. But if you’re asking whether there’s some specific ongoing practical problem, like a big financial crisis or a new living situation I’m still trying to manage, I’m not sure I can point to one clearly.

A lot of the obvious things, I guess, are more settled than they were at first. But day to day it still feels different because I’m the one here, and I’m the one who has to notice things and decide things. I don’t know if that counts as an “active stressor” or just life now. That’s where I get a little stuck answering you.

So… I wouldn’t want to say there’s one particular practical change that’s still driving everything. It’s more that I don’t know what part is practical and what part is just the fact that my life changed.
Aside from this physical urge to move, do you also feel tense, nervous, or on edge, or find yourself worrying a lot, especially since your husband passed away?

I’m not sure I’d call it worry, exactly. I mean, I do get… unsettled, but it feels more in my body than in my thoughts, if that makes sense. Like I’m not always sitting there thinking, “What if this happens, what if that happens.” It’s more like I can’t relax into the chair or into the room.

Since he passed, I guess there are moments where I feel thrown off, but I don’t know that I’m walking around feeling nervous all the time. I’m not sure I can separate “on edge” from that restless feeling I was describing. They kind of blur together for me. I wouldn’t want to say I’m worrying a lot in a specific way, because I don’t really know if that’s what’s happening. It’s more just… I can’t seem to settle.

No depressive mood/anhedonia, no medication exposure to suggest akathisia, and no complicated grief/preoccupation pattern reported, so prolonged duration argues against typical adjustment disorder but no new disorder is clearly supported yet; candidates unchanged pending clarification on ongoing stressors.

doctor.intent: Determine whether concrete, ongoing life changes or stressor-related circumstances from her husband's death (e.g., financial, living situation, new responsibilities) are still actively present, versus the stressor having largely resolved while the restlessness persists independently—this helps distinguish a prolonged adjustment disorder tied to an ongoing stressor from a separate, self-sustaining stress reaction.
doctor.question: Right now, are there still specific practical changes from your husband's death—like new financial responsibilities, living arrangements, or day-to-day roles—that you're actively dealing with, or has most of that settled down at this point?

target_item.reason: The question asks about ongoing practical life changes or responsibilities related to the husband's death, which is a contextual stressor issue rather than one of the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know how to separate that out, honestly. I mean, there are still… things that are different because he’s not here, of course. But if you’re asking whether there’s some specific ongoing practical problem, like a big financial crisis or a new living situation I’m still trying to manage, I’m not sure I can point to one clearly.

A lot of the obvious things, I guess, are more settled than they were at first. But day to day it still feels different because I’m the one here, and I’m the one who has to notice things and decide things. I don’t know if that counts as an “active stressor” or just life now. That’s where I get a little stuck answering you.

So… I wouldn’t want to say there’s one particular practical change that’s still driving everything. It’s more that I don’t know what part is practical and what part is just the fact that my life changed.

doctor.intent: Assess whether core anxiety symptoms (nervousness, worry, edge feelings) are present alongside the physical restlessness, which would support an adjustment disorder with anxiety rather than another stress-related pattern lacking prominent anxious cognition.
doctor.question: Aside from this physical urge to move, do you also feel tense, nervous, or on edge, or find yourself worrying a lot, especially since your husband passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anxiety symptoms such as feeling tense, nervous, on edge, or worrying a lot, especially in relation to bereavement. The provided symptom profile covers ADHD symptoms and related impairment/duration, but does not include a specific anxiety or worry item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it worry, exactly. I mean, I do get… unsettled, but it feels more in my body than in my thoughts, if that makes sense. Like I’m not always sitting there thinking, “What if this happens, what if that happens.” It’s more like I can’t relax into the chair or into the room.

Since he passed, I guess there are moments where I feel thrown off, but I don’t know that I’m walking around feeling nervous all the time. I’m not sure I can separate “on edge” from that restless feeling I was describing. They kind of blur together for me. I wouldn’t want to say I’m worrying a lot in a specific way, because I don’t really know if that’s what’s happening. It’s more just… I can’t seem to settle.

inference.note: Patient denies significant anxious worry/nervousness separate from the physical restlessness, and denies prominent depressive symptoms, making generalized anxiety and depressive-predominant reactions less likely. Symptoms remain a persistent, purely somatic restlessness that began after bereavement and has continued nearly 2 years without clear ongoing acute stressor, consistent with prolonged grief/adjustment-type reaction (F43.8) or persistent depressive/adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct/emotions (F43.21); akathisia remains unlikely given no antipsychotic/antiemetic exposure.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent, whole-body physical restlessness ('can't settle inside my own skin') that began following the death of her husband nearly two years ago and has continued essentially unremitting since, causing significant functional impairment (inability to manage responsibilities, unreliability with family/church commitments). No history of antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure or recent dose change, and the restlessness is described as bodily-driven rather than leg-localized or worse specifically at rest/night, arguing against akathisia or Restless Legs Syndrome. She denies pervasive depressed mood, anhedonia, or prominent worry/anxious cognition, and denies a pattern consistent with Prolonged Grief Disorder (not preoccupied with disbelief/yearning as the core driver, and distress is not specifically tied to reminders of the deceased). Because the identifiable psychosocial stressor (bereavement) is clear but the symptom presentation (a persistent motor restlessness syndrome) does not fit neatly into standard adjustment disorder subtypes (depressed mood, anxiety, mixed, disturbance of conduct) and has lasted well beyond the typical 6-month expected resolution after stressor termination-related criteria for adjustment disorder, this is best classified as Other Reactions to Severe Stress (F43.8), with Adjustment Disorder (F43.21) and Prolonged Grief Disorder as differentials that were considered but did not fully fit the clinical picture.
